sections.title: Connecting passive to active safety cues

toc.title: Three uses for safety cues and anchors

sections.title: 1. Self-regulating when losing access to safety
2. Self-regulating out of a traumatized state
3. Building the strength of your vagal brake

blocks.p: The word "safety" has already come up numerous times. (And it will continue to.) Let's create a shared language and begin to parse out some concepts. I will differentiate among three things:

"Safety" refers to many things. It can refer to literal external safety, like a safe environment and safe people. "Safety" can refer to your subjective emotional and cognitive experiences. But "safety" can also refer to the biological pathways responsible for social engagement, play, intimacy, and stillness. These biological pathways are the myelinated ventral vagal ones. When these pathways are active enough, we experience safety and an impulse for connection.
When I say "safety," I might refer to any of these possibilities. But at its core, "safety" refers to biology. We feel, experience, and act upon the safety biology.

Safety cues are the things that trigger the ventral vagal pathways to activate through neuroception. Safety cues can be many things, and they are highly individualized. A safety cue for me may be different for you. There are two types of safety cues: passive and active.
Passive safety cues provide you with a neuroception of safety without doing anything consciously. Passive cues are environmental or interpersonal. Examples of passive safety cues are:

ul: birds singing, and elements of nature

blocks.p: None of these require you to notice and experience them consciously. Your body detects safety cues from the external world, and then your safety state activates. When you see someone you care about, your safety state probably instantly activates. The person is a safety cue in and of themselves. More specifically, their smile and eye contact is a safety cue. Your history of safety with them is a safety cue. You don't need to set up, buy, or do anything to receive their safety. You passively do so. The same goes for environmental safety cues. When you go to a beach, the sound of the waves, the laughter of children, the sun on your skin: these all likely activate your safety state.
You don't need to mindfully experience these passive safety cues. But you could. (More on this in a bit.)

Active safety cues provide a neuroception of safety through your direct participation. You actively do something to provide your system with a cue of safety. Just like with passive cues, active cues can come in many different forms, such as:

blocks.h3: Connecting passive to active safety cues

q: "Once the passive pathway effectively shifts our physiological state, the second step can be initiated. The second step, exercising the vagal brake, recruits the active (voluntary) pathway through rituals requiring manipulation of breath, posture, and vocalization." (Porges)

blocks.p: In the quote above, Dr. Porges connects passive to active safety. The passive cues initially shift physiological state into the ventral vagal pathways. From there, one can use more active means to extend or deepen their safety cueing and even develop the strength of their vagal brake. The passive cues come first; then, we build on them actively. (The quote refers to religious rituals, but we can apply the idea generally.) In essence, active builds on passive.

You can get the most out of passive and active safety cues through mindful awareness of how they affect your system. Be mindful of safety by looking inward and noticing how a cue feels and your experience of it.

That being said, mindfulness poses a significant challenge for those stuck in a defensive state with little safety experience. This is because mindfulness is impossible when in a dysregulated defensive state: your safety pathways need to be active enough to connect with your inner world. When your body is ready for connection with your inner experience, you will feel it as openness and curiosity. Curiosity allows you to ask yourself how something affects your system. And then you can be mindful of the experience within.
"Dangit, Justin! So I'm out of luck then, you're saying?!"

Wait wait wait. I said mindfulness is impossible when you're in a dysregulated defensive state. That means when you have no noticeable safety activation. Your safety pathways need to be active enough to connect with your inner world. You just need some safety activation. Not complete, perfect, or endless safety activation.

The good news is that you already have some access to your safety state. Think about it: if you didn't, you probably wouldn't be sitting in stillness right now and reading these words. If you were in a dominantly defensive state, you'd be too anxious, angry, overwhelmed, or unmotivated to read and learn effectively. You have some access to safety. Do you have enough safety for more curiosity about your inner world? Maybe. And if not, that's okay. You're in the right place for the job!

Think of your Polyvagal states as spectrums or gradients. They have different levels of activation. Right now, you may not be able to smile and hug someone. You may not be able to feel your traumatic state compassionately. Heck, you may not even want to! But you do currently have enough safety to immobilize, read these words, focus, learn, and think critically. That's a great starting point!

You can learn to activate your safety state further and anchor into it. You'll go beyond reading and learning and into curiosity and even self-compassion. To get to this deeper level of safety, you need to go beyond safety cues and into safety anchors.

A safety anchor is the mindful experience of a passive or active safety cue. Safety anchors settle you more deeply into your safety state. They enhance and extend your existence in the present moment: your connection to yourself, the environment, and others.

A safety cue triggers your safety state passively or actively. The cue can become an anchor if you focus on how it affects your system. For example, listening to calming music in the background might be a passive cue to your safety state, helping slow you down and focus. But you can increase your safety access and settle more deeply (anchor) into the music by mindfully listening and noticing how it affects you experientially. Listening mindfully to music makes you a direct experiencer of the music rather than a passive recipient.

A safety anchor keeps us connected to our bodies and the present moment. It helps us feel more present, conscious, and aware of our senses. A safety anchor can be a movement, a hobby, a voice, a spiritual practice, a memory, an imaginative scene, or anything else that helps us to feel safe, calm, and connected. No matter the source, mindfulness of the experience is essential to anchoring into safety.

Like an anchor in the ocean floor keeps the boat from drifting away, safety anchors keep you from drifting too far into defensive states. When defensive energy ramps up and we feel ourselves drifting away from our safety state, safety anchors can help us stay grounded in the present moment and our bodies. Staying anchored to safety means you can maintain access to your present moment experience and your capacity for self-regulation.

blocks.why: A cue becomes an anchor when you notice how it affects you. This practice is built for exactly that.

blocks.h: Three uses for safety cues and anchors

blocks.p: You can use safety cues and anchors in three ways. All three are connected, building on each other in accessibility and usability.

ol: self-regulating when losing access to the safety state
self-regulating out of a stuck defensive state
building the strength of your vagal brake through repeated acts of self-regulation.

blocks.h3: 1. Self-regulating when losing access to safety

blocks.p: The first way to use safety cues and anchors is when you feel yourself drifting into a defensive state. You may be familiar with these: anxiety, anger, irritation, or numbness are examples of defensive drifting. Especially if you notice these early on, you can use cues and anchors to help pull yourself back into your body and the present moment.

It's important to use a safety anchor before it's "too late." If you wait until you are in a full-blown defensive state, it may be too difficult to use the anchor effectively. Instead, use the anchor as soon as you feel yourself drifting into a defensive state. For example, instead of waiting for a 10 out of 10 in anxiety, use a safety anchor when at a 3. Basically, when the anxiety is tolerable you still have enough safety to mindfully utilize your passive and active safety cues.

Safety cues and anchors activate your safety pathways. The activation will help you soften the intensity of your defensive state and get through mild to moderate dysregulation, especially with practice and a stronger vagal brake. Eventually, through mindful safety anchoring and repeated self-regulation practices, your vagal brake will strengthen and allow unstucking from trauma.

blocks.h3: 2. Self-regulating out of a traumatized state

blocks.p: The second way of using safety cues and anchors is to self-regulate out of a stuck defensive state. Safety anchoring creates the conditions for bottom-up ladder climbing to happen. Remember, the body must self-regulate to optimize its resources for "health, growth, and restoration," as Dr. Porges often reiterates. Developing your safety state through mindful use of safety anchors will eventually allow self-regulation.

This second use of anchoring is not for when you lose access to your safety state and then catch yourself as you descend the Polyvagal ladder like in number one above. Instead, you're already in a stuck defensive state and working your way out. This stuck defensive state is probably what brings you here. And it's probably something you've been stuck in for many years.

Think of it this way: the first use of safety anchoring is for anyone to use as a self-regulation method. This second use is for traumatized individuals to use for life-long change. It's a slower process but necessary for trauma recovery. The autonomic nervous system does not self-regulate unless it has a strong anchoring in the safety state.

This use of safety anchoring leads to the ["danger" in safety](anchor:there-is-danger-in-safety). When defensive activation surfaces, don't judge it. Just notice and let it be while you use your safety anchors passively and actively. You could also use simple coping skills to get through the moment until you can anchor back into safety.

blocks.h3: 3. Building the strength of your vagal brake

blocks.p: As a result of regularly practicing the first two, you will gradually increase the strength of your safety state. Your distress tolerance will strengthen, especially if you allow some defensive activation while grounding in safety. You don't need to conjure the defensive energy, just let it be present as it naturally emerges and further anchor yourself.

Strengthening your vagal brake means that you will eventually have less defensive state activation overall. When you do have moments of dysregulation, they will not be as all-consuming. If you've developed your vagal brake and have a strong sense of what safety anchors you can use, you will recover more quickly from dysregulation.

The vagal brake can be further strengthened by mindfully allowing and experiencing defensive activation when anchored in safety. This opens the potential for pendulation: mindfully shifting focus from safety to defense repeatedly. There's no need to worry about or take action on this for now.

Safety cues and anchors vary from person to person. The ideas I suggest may be helpful, but I don't know what will work for you in your current state. You'll need to discern what anchors you and what doesn't.

For example, dancing wouldn't work as an active safety cue for me at all. It would be counterproductive for me to try to self-regulate by dancing. I don't do it, I don't like it, and I can't stand it. (I'm the only person at a wedding, not dancing. And I'm okay with that.) But for you, dancing might be a great safety cue and even a potential anchor.

There is no one-size-fits-all to safety cues and anchors, but some things are more likely to be helpful than others. Muscle relaxation, extended exhales, and nature are likely safety cues or anchors for most people. However, these things may not be helpful for you currently. The thought of slowing down to breathe into your belly through your nose might increase your anxiety because movement would be a better fit for you. Or maybe you have severe allergies and often can't breathe through your nose, like me.

Not only are safety cues and anchors highly individualized, but they also vary by state. When you're in a flight/fight state, dancing might be perfect to climb your Polyvagal ladder. Dancing might not be a good fit for shutdown, but yoga would.

We could even go one step further by customizing cues and anchors based on your state. For example, dancing quickly and spontaneously may work for you in flight/fight. While dancing slowly and purposefully is a good fit for you in shutdown.

As you experiment, gauge what safety cues and anchors generally work for you. And if you can, notice what types of cues and anchors work for you based on what state you're in. If that's too much for you, then keep it general. I recommend you list cues and anchors that you find generally beneficial for now. Practice what is on your list to identify what is effective and when.

blocks.prompt: What are three cues or anchors that seem to work for you? Do any work better in one state than another?

blocks.p: As the safety state develops and strengthens, defensive activation may accompany it. I've seen this tag-along defense in my client work and heard it from [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) students and the podcast audience. It's bound to happen to some degree. Why is this?

Because the vagal brake is stronger and allows for natural self-regulation. The autonomic nervous system gets the message that it's time to climb the Polyvagal ladder and settle into safety. The body is attempting to self-regulate and return to its natural homeostatic functioning. The body is compelled toward self-regulation and homeostasis. And that means Polyvagal ladder climbing, which means shifting out of stuck defensive states. At least, attempting to.

If you notice defensive state activation, don't worry. It's a normal part of the process. At this point, I would recommend using simple coping skills to ride through it. Either that or use the new safety cues and anchors you develop.

You don't need to "sit with it" during this phase. You don't need to "feel your feelings" either. For now, just notice the defensive state activation and allow it to be there. Imagine putting it into a jar or your pocket and letting it exist. Then, use a coping skill, a safety cue, or a safety anchor.

You could even reframe defensive state activation as evidence of success. For example, feeling anxiety may be an indication of returning sympathetic energy. If it's your typical nightly dysregulated anxiety, then it's probably not a sign of progress. But if you're generally experiencing more safety activation and making progress, then accompanying anxiousness may be a good sign.

Focus on safety for now. And focus on it consistently. If defensive activation occurs, continually focus and prioritize safety or coping to get through the moment. However, don't "white-knuckle" safety. If you're going through a mini-crisis, like a panic attack, focus on getting through it with whatever coping skills you usually use. For more severe dysregulation, continue to consult with and seek professional assistance.
